entry.title: Report: AI companies buy, scan, and destroy millions of physical books to train models, risking permanent loss of public knowledge [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Several AI companies are purchasing large quantities of secondhand books, scanning them for training data, and then destroying the physical copies to prevent competitors from accessing the material and to avoid legal risks. This practice has raised ethical concerns as it locks human knowledge inside private servers and removes valuable cultural heritage from the public domain. Anna's Archive, a major shadow library, is calling for volunteers worldwide to scan and upload rare and at-risk books to preserve human knowledge before it disappears. The group warns that as AI-generated content dominates new publications, preserving original human-written materials is critical to maintaining the diversity and authenticity of human civilization's recorded knowledge.

entry.title: Developer launches Huzzah, an experimental editor using persistent pseudocode prompts to improve AI-assisted coding workflows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A software engineer introduced Huzzah, a new coding tool that replaces traditional longform, imperative AI prompts with persistent, declarative pseudocode to generate and update code. This approach aims to provide clearer human intent records, reduce repetitive instructions, and improve efficiency compared to existing AI coding agents. Huzzah allows developers to write concise pseudocode files that serve as both prompts and documentation, automatically regenerating source code upon saving changes. The tool is designed primarily for new codebases and may face challenges with complex dependencies or scaling, but it offers a more structured and readable alternative to natural language prompts in AI-assisted software development.

entry.title: OpenRouter.ai launches Ox Alpha, a new AI model available for public testing
entry.summary: OpenRouter.ai has introduced Ox Alpha, a new AI model designed for public use and testing. The release aims to provide developers and researchers with access to advanced AI capabilities through an open platform. The launch has sparked community discussion and feedback on Hacker News, reflecting interest in its potential applications and performance.

entry.title: Vomit: Open-source tool uses local LLM to clean up Claude 5's token output into readable English without external dependencies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Vomit is an open-source tool that processes Claude 5's token output by piping it through a local language model to convert it into readable English. It operates fully locally without telemetry or external dependencies, though it may hallucinate due to limited input and runs slowly. The tool is primarily tested on Mac and offers both invasive and non-invasive modes to translate Claude's session outputs, supporting local LLMs like Llama.app and Ollama. Users can install Vomit via Go and configure it to replace or monitor Claude's output, with the source code available under the GNU GPLv3 license.

entry.title: Blog argues anti-AI fonts that scramble text harm accessibility and are ineffective against AI scraping [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A blog post published in August 2026 critiques the concept of "anti-AI" fonts designed to obfuscate or scramble text to prevent AI scraping. The author argues these fonts create accessibility issues for disabled users relying on screen readers and other tools, and that AI companies are already developing ways to bypass such obfuscations. The post suggests that attempts to selectively restrict metadata access could lead to privacy and security concerns, and that widespread use of obfuscation could result in costly, restrictive web environments contrary to the open nature of the internet. The author highlights that no accessible solution currently exists because accessible content requires machine-readable metadata, which conflicts with obfuscation goals. They also note that more elaborate anti-AI techniques, such as motion graphics, are impractical for everyday web use and will likely be circumvented over time. Ultimately, the post concludes that all publicly available information will become accessible to AI systems, and efforts to block this are futile and potentially harmful to web openness and accessibility.

entry.title: Researchers propose active inference framework for AI agents to efficiently acquire context through optimal question asking and prompt optimization under token budgets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present a model-agnostic active inference framework that enables interactive AI agents to efficiently acquire context by balancing clarifying questions, retrievals, and default assumptions. The approach updates beliefs over latent task states and selects actions to minimize expected free energy, incorporating token costs and information gain. The framework is instantiated in Optimal Question Asking (OQA) with exact posteriors and dynamic programming, and benchmarked on language models across tasks with 25 to 300 candidates. The study also explores clarification before generation and automated prompt optimization, positioning active inference as a design principle for AI context acquisition layers.

entry.title: PolicyGuide compiles domain policies into workflow graphs to guide LLM agents through multi-step procedures, improving policy compliance across airline, retail, and telecom domains [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: PolicyGuide addresses compliance failures in customer-service large language model (LLM) agents by compiling organizational policies into workflow graphs and using a proactive verifier to guide agents through multi-step procedures. This approach improves adherence to policy by reconciling open requests and providing step-specific remediation at user-turn boundaries. Evaluations with GPT-5.4 agents across airline, retail, and telecom domains show an increase in compliance metrics, with the largest improvement in the telecom domain. The workflows also transfer effectively to other LLM agents like Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 2.5 Pro. Additional tests demonstrate reduced attack success rates under adversarial conditions and strong procedural compliance in workflow-level validations.

entry.title: Researchers propose EnvHarness, a programmable layer that reshapes static environments for LLM agent learning without altering underlying logic, improving performance across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce EnvHarness, a programmable layer of plug-in components that wraps static environments to modify their behavior without changing the original environment logic, addressing limitations of hand-built, static environments in LLM agent learning. EnvHarness operates through standard interfaces, retains original verifiers, and applies across diverse domains. To automate environment reshaping, they present EnvRigger, which analyzes agent execution trajectories to identify flaws and synthesize EnvHarness components, validating improvements through new rollouts. Across five benchmarks in four domains, EnvHarness outperforms original environments and domain-specific generation pipelines, achieving up to a 9.0-point improvement with 9.8% fewer execution steps. The approach also enhances reinforcement learning by providing a better optimization signal, enabling continuous co-evolution of policies and environments.

entry.title: Researchers introduce MemTrapBench to evaluate cognitive traps in LLM memory use, finding all tested memory strategies reduce task performance by over 10% compared to no-memory settings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed MemTrapBench, a benchmark designed to assess how memory in large language models (LLMs) can induce cognitive traps that distort reasoning and degrade task performance. The benchmark focuses on two types of cognitive traps: Reasoning Fixation and Belief Distortion. Experiments across multiple model families and memory frameworks revealed that all evaluated memory strategies underperform compared to models without memory, with performance drops exceeding 10%. To address these issues, the team proposed AdaptiveMem, an inference-time method that helps LLMs avoid memory traps while maintaining or improving results on standard memory benchmarks across various frameworks.

entry.title: AI4AI-Bench introduces a benchmark for LLM agents to redesign training algorithms for recursive self-improvement across 10 tasks with limited success [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: AI4AI-Bench presents a new benchmark to evaluate whether large language model agents can improve training algorithms, a key aspect of recursive self-improvement in AI systems. The benchmark includes 10 frozen research repositories representing different training algorithm families, where agents have limited time to rewrite algorithms that are then rerun and scored against original versions. Results show that even the best systems achieve only a fraction of the optimal improvement, with most agents not altering the learning process significantly. The benchmark suite, evaluators, and scored submissions are publicly released to enable ongoing measurement and progress tracking in this area.

entry.title: Researchers present Asymmetric Attention Heads, a transformer attention method allocating context length per head to improve validation loss over full attention in 4096-token experiments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Asymmetric Attention Heads (AAH), a framework that assigns different context lengths to individual or grouped attention heads in transformers, reflecting their distinct contextual roles. AAH organizes heads hierarchically and applies causal local windows while maintaining the standard multi-head attention output interface. Experiments with 4096-token sequences show that several AAH variants achieve lower validation loss compared to standard full attention. Ablation studies indicate that stable local allocation and structured head-window assignments are important, with fixed or local controls sometimes matching adaptive hierarchies. The approach includes a diagnostic metric called Attention Coverage Ratio to analyze window routing and context allocation quality.

entry.title: Researchers propose time-series retrieval to improve multimodal large language models for remaining useful life estimation in prognostics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers investigate the use of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) grounded through time-series retrieval to estimate remaining useful life (RUL) in prognostics and health management (PHM). They introduce a framework that retrieves similar historical degradation segments and transforms them with test data into visual comparison artifacts processed by MLLMs via structured multimodal prompts. The approach is evaluated on the FD001 partition of the C-MAPSS benchmark, showing that retrieval-based inference consistently improves RUL prediction accuracy and stability compared to non-retrieval baselines, with benefits depending on model capacity. The study highlights that time-series retrieval augmented generation (RAG) is a promising method for enhancing multimodal prognostic reasoning but also notes current limitations of MLLM-based RUL estimation in practical PHM applications. The results suggest that retrieval is most effective when the underlying MLLM can effectively utilize the retrieved evidence, indicating a dependency on model capability for performance gains.

entry.title: Researchers develop efficient statistical model to estimate uncertainty dynamics in large language model text generation, reducing costly resampling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers address the high computational cost of resampling text sequences in large language model (LLM) reasoning by developing a statistical model that smooths noisy low-sample rollout data to better approximate high-sample data. Their work reveals that uncertainty dynamics in LLM reasoning converge to stable patterns and that much of the observed noise is due to sampling artifacts rather than sensitivity to individual tokens or reasoning steps. This approach significantly reduces the sampling costs involved in analyzing the distribution of reasoning chains produced by LLMs for given questions.

entry.title: Researchers propose TUP method to improve Best-of-N distillation by truncating low-ranked completions and upweighting high-ranked ones with offline training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce TUP (Truncate-bad, Upweight-good Policy), a method that enhances inference-time selection in generative models by removing low-ranked completions and reweighting only the upper tail with adjustable sharpness. TUP uses a closed-form normalization independent of prompts and can be trained offline using binary cross-entropy with shifted-truncated win-rates as soft labels and distilled log-likelihood ratios as logits. Theoretical analysis supports truncating the lower tail rather than merely downweighting it, and empirical results show TUP performs competitively with strong offline alignment baselines.

entry.title: Researchers audit step-level credit assignment methods in LLM agents against causal ground truth from executed replay in ALFWorld, finding none outperform chance in identifying causally pivotal steps [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated common step-level credit signals used to train large language model (LLM) agents-such as LLM-judge scores, outcome-conditioned log probability ratios, and policy confidence-against causal ground truth derived from executed replay in the ALFWorld environment. They found these signals fail to identify which decision steps causally affect outcomes better than chance, contrasting with prior evaluations based on annotated step correctness rather than causal contribution. The study revealed that causal contribution is sparse and model-dependent, with significant variation in measurable effects across similar policies. The failure mode is linked to implicit credit correlating with policy fluency rather than causal impact, and conditioning on outcomes adds no causal information. A confidence-only routing approach recovers pivotal steps at chance level but reduces judge evaluation costs. A pre-registered training experiment showed no credit assignment method reliably outperforms an untrained policy, with differences explained by training dose rather than credit content. The findings suggest that comparisons of credit assignment rules must control for effective sample size to avoid conflating training dose with credit quality.

entry.title: Researchers propose MileGPO for milestone inference in long-horizon reinforcement learning, improving credit assignment without auxiliary models or extra environment interaction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce MileGPO (Milestone Inference with Local Evidence for Graph-Based Policy Optimization), a method designed to improve credit assignment in long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning by identifying meaningful intermediate milestones and traps from grouped on-policy rollouts. MileGPO uses three components-Milestone Discovery, Reliability-Calibrated Shaping, and Progress-Contrastive Calibration-to weight and validate candidate milestones based on outcome confidence and local progress, without requiring auxiliary models or additional environment interaction. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that MileGPO achieves state-of-the-art performance with a small gap between in-distribution and out-of-distribution results on ALFWorld. Ablation studies and credit diagnostics show that combining reliability weighting, local progress assessment, and same-state branch evidence enhances milestone discovery and resolves ambiguous intermediate credit assignment.

entry.title: Researchers propose compute-efficient hyperparameter transfer method for large-scale Mixture-of-Experts models, enabling learning rate extrapolation to trillion-token training horizons [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce a two-step hyperparameter transfer framework to optimize learning rates for large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models efficiently. The method transfers optimal learning rates across model widths using Maximal Update Parameterization and Multi-head Latent Attention, then extrapolates these rates to extensive token budgets via a predictive scaling law derived from small proxy models. Applying this approach, the team pretrained a 155-billion-parameter foundation model with 17 billion active parameters, demonstrating stable training and accurate prediction of optimal configurations with minimal computational cost. This suggests that small-scale proxy training can effectively guide hyperparameter tuning for massive MoE models, reducing the need for costly large-scale sweeps.

entry.title: Task-CoEvolve introduces adaptive validation task selection to optimize LLM agent harnesses, reducing evaluation costs by 80% while maintaining performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Task-CoEvolve is a new method for optimizing large language model (LLM) agent harnesses by adaptively selecting validation tasks during iterative harness code rewriting. Unlike existing methods that evaluate a fixed validation set fully at each iteration, Task-CoEvolve focuses on tasks where candidate harnesses disagree, using variance-weighted sampling to prioritize informative tasks near the agent's capability frontier and estimating full-set performance from partial evaluations. Experiments on online text classification and Terminal-Bench 2.1 demonstrate that Task-CoEvolve matches the performance of full-set search while significantly reducing the number of evaluations needed during optimization. The authors plan to release the code publicly.

entry.title: Researchers release Daedalus-150M, a convolution-attention hybrid language model optimized for CPU inference with 4-bit weights and improved speed and efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers developed Daedalus-150M, a small language model designed specifically for CPU inference using 4-bit weights and a hybrid architecture combining full attention in 6 of 18 blocks with short convolutions in the rest. Trained from scratch on 59.9 billion tokens, it outperforms several similarly sized models trained on more data, achieving a 47.31 score on a five-task benchmark and faster decoding speeds with lower memory usage. The model's architecture reduces memory demands by limiting convolutional memory to two timesteps, avoiding re-reading a growing cache in most blocks. Compared to a conventional all-attention model of the same size and training data, Daedalus-150M showed a 0.81% improvement in quality metrics, a 6.3% smaller 4-bit file size, and up to 2.08 times faster decoding at longer context lengths. The researchers also noted challenges including quality costs from 4-bit quantization, inactive convolution channels, and an oversized vocabulary for the model size.

entry.title: Researchers introduce HN-CLIP with adaptive similarity margins for dense-caption retrieval, improving accuracy by up to 4% and training speed by over 2x on four benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed HN-CLIP, a method that uses a text encoder's own similarity matrix to assign adaptive margins to negative samples in dense-caption retrieval tasks. This approach addresses premature saturation in the commonly used InfoNCE objective caused by near-duplicate captions, without requiring additional data or complex preprocessing. Experiments on four benchmarks show HN-CLIP improves retrieval accuracy by 2.5 to 4.0 percentage points in R@1 and trains significantly faster than leading methods like GOAL and StructXLIP. The method also enhances six fine-tuning frameworks and achieves top baseline performance using only 20% of the training data.

entry.title: Investigating the Interplay between Contextual and Parametric Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness under Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2605.24960v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) faithfulness, i.e., whether CoTs genuinely reflect large language models' (LLM) underlying behavior, is typically evaluated with metrics under two disjoint paradigms: contextual faithfulness, measured by perturbing the input or CoT trace, and parametric faithfulness, assessed by intervening on a model's parametric knowledge. Yet prior work compares them only descriptively. We fill this gap by proposing FaithMATE, a unified preference-alignment interface for optimizing models towards either faithfulness paradigm. It enables us to investigate the interplay between the two paradigms, examining whether and to what extent faithfulness gains generalize within and across paradigms. Across three models, two datasets, and six faithfulness metrics, we find that the two paradigms are positively coupled, yet asymmetric: optimizing towards parametric faithfulness yields consistent gains across both paradigms, whereas the contextual counterpart delivers more variable gains. Within the contextual paradigm, faithfulness gains on one metric do not consistently transfer to others, implying that existing contextual metrics capture disjoint facets of faithfulness and exposing inherent trade-offs. These findings imply that CoT faithfulness is not a monolithic objective and therefore requires multifaceted optimization and evaluation.

entry.title: Ask to Be Sure: Informative Interactions for Confident Multi-Turn LLM Recommendation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.15949v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled their use as conversational recommender systems (CRS), demonstrating strong recommendation accuracy and natural dialogue. However, guiding multi-turn interactions to elicit user preferences effectively remains challenging. Existing approaches either use separate reinforcement learning agents with templated interactions or optimize for interactivity judged by another LLM, without measuring how much useful information is actually gained. We propose a new approach that quantifies the effectiveness of each interaction by the reduction in the assistant's uncertainty, measured via entropy over recommendations. We apply this entropy reduction as a reward---without relying on ground-truth recommendations, which are often unavailable in real-world scenarios---to fine-tune the LLM, enabling strategic interaction generation. Empirical results with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO) on the INSPIRED and ReDial datasets show that our method improves both recommendation quality and conversational efficiency.

entry.title: Graphical Design of Interpretable Architectures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.18936v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Designing, implementing, and comparing interpretable architectures requires a formal language to represent them. The most common representations fall short in one of two ways. Symbolic equations give no global view of an architecture at a glance. Probabilistic graphical models and flowcharts do not describe actual tensor manipulations, thus hiding key insights and limiting reproducibility. To close this gap, we introduce a graphical notation for designing interpretable AI architectures, adapted from Penrose tensor notation. This graphical notation gives a global view of an architecture and maps one to one onto PyTorch einsum code. We first use this notation to describe architectures that are interpretable by construction, including concept bottlenecks, sparse probes, prototype networks, neural additive models, and mixtures of linear models. We then diagram the key architectural components of Steerling-8B, a frontier interpretable language model. The diagram yields global insights into the architecture (e.g., showing that Steerling is a residual model), a geometric interpretation of each individual operation, and a direct translation into 33 lines of PyTorch code.
